694.title: Where it didn't
694.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism look honestly at where it hasn't helped, and pair it with other support, such as friends, counseling, rest or a faith community.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Discourses, where progress shows in how you meet the day. Your line was it worked here.

Nobody makes a poster of this part. Three in the morning, a year into the practice, someone lies awake who knows all the lines by now. Some things are up to us, some aren't. It isn't the thing, it's the judgment about the thing. They could recite them in their sleep, if they could sleep. And none of it is loosening the knot in the chest. The words sit there like a poster on a waiting-room wall. Yesterday was where the porch helped. Today, just as plainly: where it didn't.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `ALL THE LINES, NO SLEEP.` → `WHERE IT DIDN'T HELP.`

segments.voice: First, the Stoics saw this coming. In the Discourses, Epictetus challenges his students: show me a Stoic, if you can. Not someone who can talk Stoic, but someone who is sick and happy, in danger and happy, disgraced and happy. He says he'd gladly see one, and implies he hasn't. And Marcus expects to be knocked out of tune. When circumstances force you to be disturbed, he writes, come back to yourself quickly, and don't stay out of tune longer than you must. The teachers didn't claim the method always worked, even on them. Second, where it can misfire. When it turns into small-s stoic: teeth gritted, feelings pushed down until they come out sideways. When up to us and not up to us becomes an excuse to shrug at something you could change, or something unfair that someone should challenge. And when the trouble is depression, a deep loss, or a body that needs care. A maxim is not a doctor, a friend, or a night's sleep. Third, two honest reasons. Sometimes the tool was fine and you were hungry, exhausted, or alone. Sometimes it was the wrong tool for the job. Both are worth knowing, and neither is a failure of character. Fourth, why say it out loud. A practice that only reports its wins turns into a sales pitch. One that can say here, it didn't help stays a practice, something you use with open eyes.

695.title: Ahead: the great questions
695.hook: year three turns to suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness and awe, across many traditions
695.howItsDone: Some people on their own spiritual path return again and again to a few great questions, reading what different traditions, philosophers and scientists say about each.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Epictetus, who asked to be shown even one true Stoic. Your line was honest about it.

Some questions come up at four in the afternoon, between emails. Most don't. The big ones come in hospital corridors, at gravesides, on the night a baby is born, in the car after you've been let go, on a mountain when the clouds suddenly open. Why is there so much suffering? What happens when we die? Can I forgive this? Traditions all over the world have sat up late with those questions. Tomorrow the porch closes for the year. Today, a look ahead.
screen: `HOSPITAL CORRIDORS, MOUNTAINTOPS.` → `THE QUESTIONS THAT COME AT NIGHT.` → `TODAY, A LOOK AHEAD.`

segments.voice: First, the six. Year three is built around six questions: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, and awe. Not a new school this time, and not a single book. Six themes, each given room, one after another. Second, how it works. Each question gets many voices: scripture and saints, sages and poets, philosophers and scientists. Every voice is named. A line from the Psalms is the Psalms; a teaching of the Buddha is the Buddha's; a finding from a lab is the lab's. Nobody is blended into anybody else, and nobody is ranked. Where traditions see a question differently, and on death they really do, each says what it says, in its own words, and it's left there. Third, the porch comes too. The Stoics don't disappear. On death there's Marcus and the ripe olive that falls blessing the tree; on awe, Marcus again, looking down from above. In year three they take a seat at a much bigger table, one voice among many. Fourth, questions to live with. In 1903 the poet Rainer Maria Rilke wrote to a young man who had asked him for advice. Be patient, he told him, with what is still unsettled in you. Love the questions themselves. Don't chase answers you aren't ready to live yet. Live the questions now, and one day you may find, almost without noticing, that you've grown into an answer. That's the spirit of year three: not a quiz with answers in the back, but a year of good company with the hard questions.

696.title: Year two close: the porch
696.hook: the school of the porch is yours to visit any time
696.howItsDone: Some people who study the Stoics keep returning to a handful of texts, the Handbook, Seneca's letters and the Meditations, rereading them over the years as guides rather than rulebooks.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ahead: six great questions for year three. Your line was the big questions.

A porch is a strange kind of room. It has a roof, so you can shelter there. It has no front wall, so the street comes right up to it. People stop on the steps to talk, to wait out the rain, to watch the evening come in. Nobody checks a ticket. You can stay an hour or a minute, and come back whenever you like. A school of philosophy started on exactly that kind of porch, and this whole year has been spent sitting on it. Today, year two closes.
screen: `A ROOF, BUT NO FRONT WALL.` → `NOBODY CHECKS A TICKET.` → `A YEAR ON THE PORCH.`

segments.voice: First, what a porch asks of you. Zeno taught in the open, at the painted porch in Athens. Notice what that means. Nobody enrolls on a porch. You step up from the street, and you can step down again. Second, how the Handbook sends you off. Near its end, Epictetus turns to his student and asks: how long will you put it off? You are not a boy any more. The contest is now; it can't be postponed. Then he points to Socrates, who became who he was by attending to reason in everything, and says: you are not yet a Socrates, but you can live as someone who wants to be one. The book doesn't end with a diploma. It ends by pointing at today. Third, not finished, and that's fine. Nobody leaves a year of reading as a sage. Epictetus asked his students to show him even one Stoic and implied he'd never seen one; Seneca said plainly that he wasn't wise. What the porch offers instead is a direction: wanting to be the kind of person Socrates was, and taking the next step on an ordinary day. Fourth, the porch stays open. A porch has no door to lock behind you. Whatever you kept from this year, a morning intention, an evening question, a delayed reply, you can step back up onto it any day you want. Tomorrow, year three: six questions.

segments.voice: Find a step if you can, a porch, a stoop, a stair in your building, or sit in a doorway, half in and half out. Feel the roof or the sky above you and the open side in front, and let the year come as one picture: whichever teacher, line or moment stayed. Don't sort it or grade it; just sit with it, the way people sit on steps at the end of a day.

697.title: Six questions
697.hook: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe: the questions under every tradition
697.howItsDone: People who read across traditions often keep a running list of their own big questions and return to the same texts with them over the years, reading for what each text asks as well as what it answers.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Socrates, the model Epictetus points to: not yet him, but someone who wants to be. Your line was the porch stays open.

"What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" That line is a question. It sits in the eighth Psalm, in a book of prayers and songs, asked while looking up at the night sky. The old books do this: in the middle of the teaching, the text turns around and asks. Year three starts right there. Not with answers. With six questions the texts themselves ask, the ones we'll carry to each tradition this year.
screen: `WHAT IS MAN?` → `THE PSALM JUST ASKS.` → `YEAR THREE STARTS WITH QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: First, the texts ask, too. It's easy to treat scripture and old philosophy as a place to look things up, but listen to how often they speak in questions. Second, suffering and death, and the book of Job asks both. Job, sitting in the ashes, says: "Wherefore is light given to him that is in misery, and life unto the bitter in soul?" Later in the book: "If a man die, shall he live again?" Third, love, work and forgiveness. In Kahlil Gibran's The Prophet, a woman named Almitra stands up and says, "Speak to us of Love." She doesn't ask whether love matters. She asks to hear about it. On work, the Teacher in Ecclesiastes asks, "What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun?" And in Matthew's Gospel, Peter brings Jesus a question with a number in it: "Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?" Fourth, awe, which takes us back to the eighth Psalm: what is man, that thou art mindful of him? That's the sixth question, and the last block of the year. Suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe, each with its own long stretch of days, in that order. Across them we'll hear the Buddha and Job, the Gospels and Rumi, the Stoics, poets and scientists, each in its own voice. Nobody hands you an answer key. The questions come first, because an answer only means something once you know what it's answering.

698.title: Answers kept apart
698.hook: this year each tradition answers in its own voice, and we don't blend them into one
698.howItsDone: Some interfaith study groups let each tradition speak in its own texts and terms, and ask members of that tradition to explain it, rather than merging teachings into one shared answer.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was six questions: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness and awe, the shape of year three. Your line was the big six.

Squeeze every tube in a child's paint box onto one plate and stir. Red, blue, yellow, the lovely violet. What you get is brown. Each color was beautiful on its own; stirred together, they cancel each other out. Wisdom from many traditions can go the same way: a little from here, a little from there, stirred into one soft answer that nobody actually holds. This year we'll hear a great many answers. So first, a rule for how we hear them.
screen: `STIR EVERY COLOR TOGETHER.` → `YOU GET BROWN.` → `A RULE BEFORE THE FIRST ANSWER.`

segments.voice: First, a blended answer belongs to nobody. Take suffering. The Buddha names craving as where it comes from. Job, in the ashes, argues his case before God. Stir those into everything happens for a reason, and you've lost both. So every answer this year is named: the Buddha's is the Buddha's, Job's is Job's. Second, each answer comes with a life. A teaching isn't a loose sentence floating in the air. It lives inside practices, a community, a long line of people who read it and argued about it. To hear it well, hear where it lives. Third, alike is not the same. Some lines do sound close. Soon we'll hear the Dhammapada say that hatred ceases by love, and later in the year Jesus will say, love your enemies. They can sit side by side as neighbors, but one belongs to the Buddha's sayings, the other to the Sermon on the Mount, and each makes the most sense in its own house. So notice the echo, and leave each line at home. Fourth, swift to hear. The letter of James puts it plainly: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." And from a very different house, the old biographer Diogenes Laertius reports the Stoic Zeno saying that we have two ears and one mouth so that we might listen more and talk less. Two houses, two sayings, each in its own words, and neither needs the other to make its point. Together they set this year's rule: hear the answer out before you reply.

699.title: Why do we suffer?
699.hook: every tradition asks it, and each answers differently
699.howItsDone: Some people bring suffering to their own tradition's texts and teachers: Christians to the Gospels and prayer, Muslims to the Qur'an and the practice of patience, Buddhists to the four noble truths, students of Stoicism to the Handbook.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Diogenes Laertius, who records Zeno's two ears and one mouth. Your line was listen first: each answer in its own house.

A man blind from birth is sitting by the road. A teacher and his students walk past, and the students ask out loud, right there: whose fault is this? Did this man do something wrong, or did his parents? It's an old question, and a hard one to hear about yourself. When something terrible happens, the nearest reason to hand is often blame. Today, the year's first great question: why do we suffer? Four answers, each in its own voice.
screen: `A MAN BLIND FROM BIRTH.` → `WHOSE FAULT IS THIS?` → `THE FIRST GREAT QUESTION.`

segments.voice: First, the Gospel of John. The disciples ask, "Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?" And Jesus answers, "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him." Then he heals him. There's a lot in the rest of that answer, but its first word is plain: neither. The shortcut to blame is closed. Second, the Qur'an. In the second surah, God says that people will be tried with something of fear and hunger, and loss of wealth and lives and crops, and then: give glad tidings to the steadfast. Hardship, in this answer, is a test, and the response it asks for is steadfastness. The Arabic word behind it is sabr, patience that holds. Third, the Buddha. In his first teaching he names suffering, then where it comes from: a craving, a thirst, always reaching for more and for something else. We'll spend the coming days inside that answer. Fourth, the Stoic Epictetus. His Handbook says that what troubles people isn't the things that happen, but their judgments about them. Death isn't terrible, or Socrates would have thought so; the terror is in our opinion of death. A test met with patience. A thirst. A judgment. And a story where blame is refused, and the story moves on to healing. They don't line up into one tidy reply, and this year won't force them to. Each speaks for itself.
screen: `WHO SINNED? NEITHER.` · `THE QUR'AN: TRIED, AND STEADFAST.` · `THE BUDDHA: A THIRST.` · `EPICTETUS: OUR JUDGMENTS.` · then, large: `EACH ANSWERS DIFFERENTLY.`

segments.voice: Let one real weight you carry come to mind, an ache, a worry, a loss; it needn't be the heaviest, and it needn't have words yet. Then let the four answers pass by it like visitors at a bedside: a test, a thirst, a judgment, neither he nor his parents. You don't have to agree with any of them; just notice which visitor you'd let stay a little longer.

Your line: each answers differently. One question, four voices, no blending. Day six hundred ninety-nine.

700.title: Name it first
700.hook: the Buddha names suffering first, the way a doctor names an illness (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)
700.carry: stand next to it and look
700.howItsDone: Buddhists learn the four noble truths as the heart of the Buddha's first teaching, and some meditation teachers begin by asking students to notice and name their experience plainly before trying to change it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sabr, patience that holds under trial, one of four answers to why we suffer. Your line was each answers differently. Today, inside the Buddha's answer.

"It's making a noise." "What kind of noise?" "A bad one." "When does it happen?" "I don't know, sometimes." A mechanic can't do a thing with that. A grinding when you brake, a click when you turn left: once the noise has a plain name, the work can start. It's easy to treat our own troubles the other way round. We fix, we distract, we explain, and we never quite say what the noise is. The Buddha's first teaching starts somewhere else. It starts by naming.
screen: `WHAT KIND OF NOISE?` → `NAMED PLAINLY, THEN FIXED.` → `THE BUDDHA STARTS BY NAMING.`

segments.voice: First, a plain list. In the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha's first teaching lays out four noble truths, and the first is suffering, dukkha. He doesn't describe it with drama. He lists it: birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering. So are being joined with what you dislike, being parted from what you love, and not getting what you want. Second, look at that last one. Not getting what you want sits on the same list as death, without ranking. A canceled plan and a funeral can both find a place there. Third, the first task is to understand it. In the same teaching, each truth comes with its own job. Suffering is to be fully understood. Its origin is to be let go. Its ending is to be realized. The path is to be developed. So the first job the Buddha gives suffering isn't fix it, escape it or explain it away. It's understand it, all the way through. Teachers sometimes use a picture for this: a good doctor names the illness before writing the prescription. Fourth, named before it's fixed. A name is a small thing, but it changes where you stand. When the trouble is a fog, you're inside it. When it has a plain name, aging, illness, being parted from someone, not getting what I wanted, you can stand next to it and look. The cause, the ending and the path all come later. In the Buddha's order, naming comes first.
screen: `A PLAIN LIST, NO DRAMA.` · `EVEN NOT GETTING WHAT YOU WANT.` · `THE FIRST TASK: UNDERSTAND IT.` · `NAMED BEFORE IT'S FIXED.` · then, large: `NAME IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: Find one pain you're carrying right now, in the body, in a relationship, or a small frustration from this morning, and name it plainly, the way the old list does: this is worry about money; this is missing my brother; this is a sore back. No because, no should, no story; if the story starts, come back to the plain name. Then sit beside it the way you'd sit beside a friend on a bench, close but not inside their trouble.
Dukkha, the Buddha's word for suffering, from birth and aging to not getting what you want, named plainly so it can be understood. Today's word.
Your line: stand next to it and look. A plain name comes before any fix. Day seven hundred, done.
